clinicalPearls: Legionella species cause two distinct illnesses collectively termed legionellosis: Legionella pneumonia (Legionnaires' disease) and Pontiac fever; most clinical disease is driven by L. pneumophila, predominantly serotype 1 (Harrison 22e p.1269).

Almost all cases trace to waterborne exposure; aerosolizing or aspiration sources include cooling towers, fountains, water misters, HVAC systems, hot tubs/spas, ice machines, and showerheads/sinks in large premise-plumbing systems (Harrison 22e p.1270-1271).

Legionella pneumonia presents as an 'atypical pneumonia' with nonspecific onset of fever, myalgias, headache, breathlessness, and dry or productive cough; accompanying neurologic or gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion) raise the likelihood of legionellosis (Harrison 22e p.1272).

A characteristic laboratory cluster supports the diagnosis: hyponatremia and/or renal dysfunction are frequent, with elevated liver enzymes, and leukocytosis or leukopenia plus thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.1272).

Per CDC, a single confirmed Legionella case in a patient who did not leave a health care facility/campus for the 10 days before onset should trigger an outbreak investigation, because nosocomial cases may signal water-system contamination (Harrison 22e p.1270-1273).

Pontiac fever is a milder, self-limited influenza-like illness defined by the ABSENCE of pneumonia, with fever, headache, myalgias, chills, vertigo, nausea/vomiting and diarrhea; antibiotics are not required (Harrison 22e p.1273).
harrison.pathophysiology: Legionellae are aerobic gram-negative bacteria ubiquitous in aquatic environments, damp soil, and compost. Their natural hosts are amoebae and other free-living protozoa, within which they replicate intracellularly; humans are accidental hosts. They have a biphasic life cycle (a nutrient-rich replicative phase and a transmissive phase under resource scarcity) and persist in biofilms within natural and engineered water systems, including building premise plumbing where temperature and nutrients support protozoal hosts. After inhalation or aspiration of small aerosol particles, the organisms are phagocytized by alveolar macrophages and monocytes; pathogenic species evade intracellular defenses (forming Legionella-containing vacuoles, downregulating cytokine receptors, inhibiting host protein synthesis, and avoiding lysosomal degradation) and replicate. Innate pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like and NOD-like receptors) together with adaptive CD4 and CD8 T-cell responses drive interferon-gamma, TNF, and neutrophil recruitment, which can clear the pathogen but may also produce immunopathology. L. pneumophila is more cytopathogenic than most non-pneumophila species, which may underlie its association with severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1269).
additionalDifferentials: Other atypical-pneumonia pathogens, notably Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae (Harrison 22e p.1272)
infectionMimics: In immunocompromised patients, Legionella can present as pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation that mimic fungal infection, or as lung abscesses (Harrison 22e p.1273)
additionalInvestigations: Lower-respiratory culture (sputum, BAL fluid, lung tissue, or extrapulmonary sites) on cysteine-supplemented buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar is the gold standard and is essential for epidemiologic typing; growth is slow (typically 3-5 days, longer for non-pneumophila species) (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274)

Polymerase chain reaction / nucleic acid amplification (including LAMP and multiplex respiratory panels) on lower-tract specimens is more sensitive than culture and remains useful during antibiotic therapy, but does not provide serotype information and most assays target only L. pneumophila (Harrison 22e p.1274-1275)
Bronchoscopy when urinary antigen is negative and the patient cannot produce adequate sputum, or in severe disease requiring ICU care (Harrison 22e p.1273)
Serology (paired acute/convalescent titers; fourfold rise to L. pneumophila serogroup 1 confirms) has limited acute sensitivity but aids outbreak investigation (Harrison 22e p.1274)
Direct fluorescent antibody testing of sputum has low and variable sensitivity (~20-70%) and is not recommended for low-risk screening due to false positives (Harrison 22e p.1274)
redFlags: Severe pneumonia with acute respiratory failure or a sepsis-like presentation warrants testing for Legionella (Harrison 22e p.1272)
Pneumonia developing during hospitalization, after recent travel, or during a known or possible outbreak should prompt Legionella testing (Harrison 22e p.1272)
Immunosuppressed patients may lack typical features such as fever and may show radiographic progression during early therapy (Harrison 22e p.1272-1273)
harrison.prognosis: Legionella pneumonia carries significant morbidity and mortality, with most patients hospitalized and many requiring ICU admission. The reported case-fatality rate is about 10%, rising to roughly 25% in health care-associated L. pneumophila pneumonia and to approximately 30-50% in immunocompromised hosts. Delayed antibiotic treatment is associated with about a threefold higher mortality. More than a quarter of survivors of severe disease have lasting complications, including recurrent hospitalizations, acute renal failure, respiratory sequelae, and recurrent pneumonias. By contrast, Pontiac fever is self-limited, usually resolving within 3-5 days, with hospitalization, complications, and death extremely rare (Harrison 22e p.1275).
pitfalls: Urinary antigen testing detects ONLY L. pneumophila serotype 1; it gives false-negative results in most cases caused by non-serotype 1 L. pneumophila and non-pneumophila species, so a negative result does not exclude legionellosis (sensitivity for serotype 1 is ~70%, though specificity is high) (Harrison 22e p.1274).

Urinary antigen can be falsely negative very early in disease yet remain positive for months after infection (especially in immunosuppressed patients), and it cannot be used in anuric patients (Harrison 22e p.1274).

Because community-acquired pneumonia guidelines recommend empirical coverage active against Legionella, specific testing is often skipped and cultures are frequently collected only after antibiotics, reducing yield (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274).

Diagnosis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinical-prediction tools (e.g., Winthrop-University Hospital Criteria, Legionella Score) are more useful for their negative than their positive predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1272).
Routine testing is less common in children, so pediatric cases may be underreported; immunosuppressed patients may present without fever or pulmonary exam findings (Harrison 22e p.1271-1272).
harrison.severityClassification: Treatment is stratified by severity: Pontiac fever requires no antibiotics (supportive care only), whereas Legionella pneumonia is managed as mild versus moderate/severe disease. All immunosuppressed patients are considered to have moderate or severe disease and should receive IV therapy where possible; all patients needing inpatient care should receive IV therapy until improving before switching to an oral agent. CDC distinguishes health care-associated cases as presumptive (Legionella pneumonia after >=10 days continuous stay in a health care facility during the 14 days before symptom onset) versus possible (some health care exposure in that window but insufficient to meet presumptive criteria) (Harrison 22e p.1272-1275).
management: Treat Legionnaires' disease with an antibiotic active against intracellular organisms, namely a respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin or a macrolide such as azithromycin
Manage Pontiac fever supportively, as it is self-limiting and does not require antibiotics
Provide supportive care with supplemental oxygen, fluid management and respiratory support as needed
Monitor for and correct associated hyponatraemia, and track renal and hepatic dysfunction
Escalate severe pneumonia with respiratory failure to intensive care for ventilatory support
Notify public-health authorities and trigger source investigation of implicated water systems, particularly for health-care-associated cases
